newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK July purchasing managers index.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK July purchasing managers index.

text.p: Following is a selection of analysts' comments after the release of the July purchasing managers index which showed the 14th successive monthly expansion in manufacturing but the first fall in new export orders since January 1996.

"The survey clearly points to a weakening of export orders. Prospects for exports are showing signs of steady deterioration. The odd thing is that hasn't come through in the trade figures yet. The main story is that while domestic demand remains buoyant, manufacturing will continue to grow, albeit slowly. The policy dilemma remains very much at the forefront of the monetary policy committee's thinking."

"The overall output index has actually risen again and the total orders index remains well above 50. In terms of what the Bank of England thinks, they really must reflect on the strength of domestic demand. The impact of sterling must be seen as a factor but maybe not the foremost one."

"This confirms that in aggregate, UK manufacturing is still performing very well. However, the headline index masks a growing split between the domestic and exporting sectors. In particular, the exports index fell below the key 50 mark for the first time since the pound's surge. The big picture still suggests that base rates will be hiked next week. Although the performance of the manufacturing sector is no reason for more tightening, services are still booming and next week's service sector report is likely to show broad-based strength."

"The survey tells us the manufacturing sector is holding up reasonably well, notwithstanding the pressure export orders are under. Manufacturers have a genuine gripe that the pound is overvalued, but it is clear that despite this the sector is managing to grow, although obviously it is not growing anywhere as fast as the rest of the economy."

"It's inevitable that a dilemma such as the one we have at the moment will arise. But we have to look through that, you can't control the exchange rate with any certainty. Its unfortunate that manufacturing will suffer but in the long run demand is growing unsustainably fast and interest rates must be set to counter that."
